Driver & tee shots
Tee height, hitting up, the centre of the face – and staying in play.

The tee shot sets up the hole. Two things matter: avoid the big miss (out of bounds, water, trees – each costs a stroke or more) and hit it as far as you can control it. Modern statistics (Broadie) show that distance is worth more than most players think – a ball 20 m further in the light rough is often better than one in the fairway 20 m back. With the driver the ball is hit on the way up, from a high tee and from the centre of the face.
TrackMan: changing the attack angle from −5° (down) to +5° (up) can give 20–30 m more carry at the same club speed.
Rule of thumb for tee height: half of the ball above the top edge of the driver at address.
A hit 1 cm towards the toe or heel costs about 5–10 % ball speed and curves the ball (gear effect).
Each km/h of club speed is worth about 2–2.5 m of carry with the driver.

Fitness, mobility & warm-up
Warm up in 10 minutes, rotate freely, more speed, fewer injuries.

Your body sets the limits of your swing: if your upper back cannot turn, your arms take over; if your hips cannot rotate, the spine compensates. TPI (Titleist Performance Institute) calls it the body–swing connection. A few minutes of mobility and strength a day and a proper warm-up before the round give more speed, better contact and protect the back. Pain is a stop sign – ask a doctor or physio.
Low back pain is the most common golf injury; a mobile upper back (thoracic spine) and hips take load off the lower back.
A dynamic warm-up (movement, not static stretching) before the round improves club speed and the first holes.
Overspeed training (e.g. SuperSpeed) typically adds about 5–8 % club speed in 6–8 weeks.
The GolfOS Coach will later have a mobility profile (TPI-style screen) that adapts your swing goals to your body.

Reading greens
Slope, fall line and speed – where the ball really breaks.

A putt only goes in when line and speed fit together. Reading means: find the slope around the hole, the fall line (the line straight down the slope) and judge how much the ball breaks at your speed. The faster the ball, the less it breaks; the slower, the more. Most amateurs see far too little break and miss on the low side – the “amateur side”.
Dave Pelz found that amateurs typically see only about a third of the real break – and then subconsciously push the ball to make up for it.
A slope of 1 % is hardly visible, but on a 6 m putt at normal speed it moves the ball about 15–25 cm.
German club greens usually run at a stimp of about 8–10, tour greens at 12–14. The faster the green, the more the same slope breaks.
The ball breaks most at the end of its roll – the last metre around the hole decides most.
Overview first, details later
Read while you walk to the green: where is the highest and the lowest point? Where does the water run off?
Look from below the hole (the low side) – slopes are easier to see from below.
Feel the slope with your feet when you walk the line – especially halfway and near the hole.
Decide the speed first, then the line – the line belongs to a speed.
The fall line and the “clock” around the hole

Imagine the hole as the centre of a clock and water poured on the green: the water runs down the fall line. A putt from straight below (uphill along the fall line) or straight above (downhill) is straight. Putts across the fall line (at 3 and 9 o’clock) break the most. Between them the break grows from zero to the maximum.
max break
fall line
The slope runs down the page: from below the hole the putt is straight, from the side it breaks most.
Speed and break belong together
Die-in speed (ball just reaches the hole): most break, the hole is “wide”.
Firm speed (45 cm past): less break, the most putts holed overall (Pelz).
Too firm: hardly any break, but a lip-out flies far past – three-putt danger.
Downhill putts break more because the ball is slower for longer.
Aim point and start line

On a breaking putt you never aim at the hole. Pick an aim point on the high side – often expressed as “cups” (one cup = 10.8 cm) or “inside left edge / two balls outside”. Then the putt is a straight putt to that point: start line and speed, as on a straight putt. Many good putters choose a spot on the green 30–50 cm in front of the ball on that start line.
Rule: if you have to miss, miss high (the “pro side”) – a ball above the hole can still fall in, one below never.
Feeling the slope with the feet

Stand halfway between ball and hole, with your feet shoulder-width apart, straddling the line and facing the hole. Close your eyes: on which foot do you feel more pressure? That side is lower. With practice you can grade the slope: 1 (hardly), 2 (clear), 3 (strong) or as a percentage. Methods like AimPoint build a full system on this and are taught in courses.
Grain, wet greens and wind
Grain (direction of growth) matters on Bermuda grass in warm countries: shiny = down-grain (faster), dull = into the grain (slower). On bent and poa greens in Germany it plays little role.
Wet or freshly sanded greens are slower and break less; afternoon greens are often faster than in the morning dew.
Strong wind changes long putts – with the wind faster, against it slower.
In Mallorca and Spain greens are often grassed with Bermuda or bent and on clay soil – read the grain near the hole.
GolfOS green slope
In Rounds the green slope map shows arrows from laser terrain data. Use it to learn: read the putt yourself first, then compare with the map – and note where you were wrong.

Irons & approach shots
Ball first, then turf: low point, contact and your real distances.

With irons you hit the ball on the way down: first the ball, then the ground in front of it – the divot starts after the ball. That is the one thing that separates good iron players from the rest. The second is knowing your real distances: most amateurs overestimate their iron carry by 10–15 m and end up short of the green. Mark Broadie’s strokes-gained research shows that the approach game makes the biggest difference between a tour player and an amateur.
Tour players hit their 7-iron with an attack angle of about −4° (down) and the low point 5–10 cm in front of the ball.
Broadie: about 40 % of the strokes a tour player gains on an amateur come from approach shots – more than from putting.
Most amateur misses on approach shots are short – take one club more when in doubt, and aim at the middle of the green.
A 10 m gap in distance between irons is normal (about 10–12 m per club for men, 8–10 m for women).
Contact: ball first

At impact the hands are slightly ahead of the ball, the shaft leans forward, most of the weight is on the lead foot. The club still moves down – the loft is delivered “compressed”. The divot starts in front of the ball and points to the target. If your divot starts behind the ball, the low point is too early (fat shot); if there is no divot and the ball flies thin, the body has moved up or back.

Mental game & routine
A routine that holds under pressure, focus on the shot, letting go of mistakes.

A round has about 90–100 strokes and takes four hours – you swing for less than three minutes. What you do in the rest of the time decides a lot: how you prepare a shot, how you commit to it and how you deal with a bad one. Good players are not free of nerves; they have a routine that carries them when the pressure rises, and they let go of a bad shot before the next one.
Vision54 (Pia Nilsson, Lynn Marriott): separate the “think box” (behind the ball: decide) from the “play box” (at the ball: only feel and target). Cross the decision line only when you have decided.
A routine of the same length (often 20–30 seconds) is a sign of good players – under pressure it stays the same.
Box breathing (4 s in, 4 s hold, 4 s out, 4 s hold) calms the heart rate in under a minute.

Pitching & wedges
20 to 100 m: the clock system, your own distance chart and the lob.

A pitch flies high and rolls little – for distances between a chip and a full wedge, or when something is in the way (bunker, rough, water). Most amateurs have only one wedge distance: a full swing. Everything shorter is guessed. Good players have a system: a few fixed swing lengths per wedge, each with a known carry. Then a 55-metre shot is no longer a feel shot but a choice from the chart.
Dave Pelz’s clock system: backswing to 7:30, 9:00 and 10:30 (lead arm as the hour hand) with the same rhythm – three distances per wedge, twelve with four wedges.
As a start value a 10:30 swing flies about 80 % and a 9:00 swing about 60 % of the full wedge distance – the same values the GolfOS caddie uses.
Tour players hit their wedges from 90 m to about 5–6 m from the hole on average; a handicap 20 player to about 12–15 m.
The biggest killer in the short game is deceleration – a long backswing and a short, slowing follow-through.
The pitch set-up
Stance a little narrower than for a full swing, slightly open.
Ball in the middle; weight about 55–60 % on the lead foot.
Grip down 2–3 cm for control.
Arms hang loose, the body turns – the arms do not lift the club.
The clock system

Imagine you stand in the middle of a clock face, head at 12. Your lead arm is the hour hand. A swing “to 9 o’clock” means: lead arm parallel to the ground. Use the same rhythm for every length – only the length of the backswing changes – and always swing through to a full, balanced finish. Measure the carry of each length with each wedge and write it down: that is your wedge chart.
Three backswing lengths, one rhythm, always a full finish.
Example (PW full 105 m): 10:30 ≈ 84 m, 9:00 ≈ 63 m, 7:30 ≈ 40 m. Your numbers will differ – measure them.
Your wedge chart

Write a small chart: rows = wedges (PW, GW, SW, LW), columns = 7:30, 9:00, 10:30, full. Measure on a range with a launch monitor or by pacing on a field (carry, where the ball lands). Enter the values under Profile → My bag → Pitches, then the caddie in Rounds suggests the right swing.
The motion
The body turns back and through; the arms stay in front of the chest.
The wrists hinge naturally on the way back and keep the angle a little through impact.
Ball first, then a shallow divot or a brush of grass in front of the ball.
Finish: chest to the target, weight on the lead foot – hold it.
Lob and flop

When there is little green between you and the hole (short-sided), over a bunker: open the face of the SW or LW before you take the grip, widen the stance, ball forward, and swing along your body line with speed – the bounce (the rounded sole) slides under the ball. It is a risky shot: practise it a lot before you play it on the course, and choose it only when no lower shot works.
Spin
Spin needs clean, dry contact: grooves and ball clean, a fairway lie, ball first.
From the rough grass gets between face and ball – less spin, more roll (“flyer”).
Soft urethane balls spin more than hard two-piece balls around the green.
Every pitch a different length
Good contact, but the length is random.
Changing speed instead of swing length; no reference values.
Clock system with one rhythm; your own wedge chart.
Fat or thin pitches
Ground before ball, or the leading edge hits the ball’s middle.
Arms-only swing, weight back, flicking the wrists at the ball.
Feet together, towel under the arms – the body turns the club.
Slowing down at the ball
Big backswing, little follow-through, short and fat.
Backswing too long for the distance – the brain brakes.
Shorter backswing, full finish – 9-to-3 drill.

Precise landing for pitches over trouble.
Lay a towel 15, 20 and 25 m away (or on the green beyond a bunker).
5 pitches to each towel; the ball must land on the towel.

Flop shot over the bag
High, soft shot with an open face – the emergency shot.
LW or SW, a golf bag as obstacle
Put your bag 3 m in front of you as an obstacle, a target 8 m away. Good lie only (ball sitting up).
Open the face first, then grip. Wide stance, ball forward, weight centred.
Long, relaxed swing with speed – the sole slides under the ball, the face stays open (pointing at the sky in the finish).
Count balls over the bag that stop within 3 m of the target.

How to practise
Block and random practice, games with scores, the right split of your time.

Most golfers practise the way they enjoy – drivers on the range – and play the way they did not practise. Good practice has a goal, feedback and pressure. Use block practice (many balls, one shot) for a technical change, then random practice (every ball different) to make it hold on the course. And spend your time where you lose strokes: most amateurs lose more around and on the greens than with the driver.
Motor learning research: random practice feels worse during practice but is remembered and transferred better.
A common split for amateurs: about 50 % short game and putting, 30 % approach, 20 % tee shots.
Short focused sessions (30–45 minutes) 2–3 times a week beat one long session.
Count and log results – without numbers you do not know whether you are getting better.
